newsitem.title: INDIA: EXPERTS GIVE INDIA STERLITE A CLEAN CHIT.
newsitem.headline: EXPERTS GIVE INDIA STERLITE A CLEAN CHIT.

text.p: Experts have cleared Sterlite India Ltd of a charge that its copper smelter pits were behind a suspected gas leak and recommended that the plant be reopened, officials said on Wednesday.

In a report released on Tuesday night, the experts said there had been no leak of sulphur dioxide from the 100,000-tonne annual capacity plant based at the port town of Tuticorin in the southern state of Tamil Nadu.
"Sterlite Industries had been operating within the parameters and conditions prescribed by the state pollution control board," said the report.
A Sterlite spokesman told Reuters the company had received no official communication about the government's move.
"We are happy that our name has been cleared but we are still waiting for the formal orders from the government," the spokesman said.
In July, Sterlite was asked to close down the smelter after suspected gas emissions affected more than 100 women workers in a nearby factory.
The report by four experts from Annamalai University said that if a gas leak had occurred at the smelter, it should have first affected Sterlite employees before spreading to nearby factories.
The report identified the neighbouring Ramesh Flowers as a possible source of the suspected gas leak where 124 women workers fell ill with symptoms of sulphur dioxide poisioning on July 5.
On Monday, state Environment Minister N.K.K. Periasamy told reporters that a decision would be taken on reopening the smelter within two days.
"The (state's) chief minister will announce the government's decision on reopening the plant within two days," he said.
The company has strongly denied any leak.
Periasamy said the authorities would now investigate if the gas had leaked from any other neighbouring factory.
Sterlite operates India's only private-sector copper smelter, which began production in December 1996.
Company officials have said that the closure was costing the company 25 million rupees ($700,000) a day. ($1=35.7 rupees)
